paras: The whipping death of a farm laborer in Lincoln County, Georgia, took place in 1885, before July 29, when two sons of the planter Joseph Dill gave 500 lashes to a Black man who had demanded his unpaid wages. He died soon afterward; an inquest called it murder, but the grand jury ignored the bill. The New York Freeman cited the case among Georgia's unpunished killings of Black people.

According to a special dispatch to the Louisville Commercial, the man had worked six months for a "well-to-do farmer" named Canady without drawing his pay. He and a fellow laborer quit and asked for their wages; Canady refused to pay in full and told them to leave.

Days later the man returned, expecting to be paid, but Canady went into the house for his gun, and the man escaped. Canady's cousin Joseph Dill, a planter "said to be worth $10,000," had two sons, Peter and David, who in the dispatch's words "decided to punish the runaway colored man" and induced him to meet them. The surviving text breaks off there and resumes with the brothers desisting, in a passage naming "the elder Canada and the elder Dill," after 500 lashes; the man died soon after.
An inquest jury pronounced the death murder, but the grand-jury foreman, a relative of the Dills and Canadys, reportedly got the bill ignored, and the brothers went free.

The only account ran on August 8, 1885, on the front page of the New York Freeman, a Black weekly, in a Louisville correspondence column headed "Bloodthirsty Kentucky. Turn on the Light." A subhead read "A Brutal Murder Ignored by the Grand Jury," and the correspondent placed the case in "the long list of unpunished murderers in Georgia." The column called the brothers "young savages" and "young brutes"; no white-paper report of the killing, nor the Louisville Commercial dispatch itself, appears in the coverage.

bases: A1 reports that two sons of a planter, cousins of the farmer who refused a Black laborer his wages, lured the laborer after he returned to demand his pay and whipped him; he died afterward.

accounts.label: Special dispatch to the Louisville Commercial (as paraphrased by the Freeman)
accounts.gist: A laborer cheated of six months' wages returned to ask for his pay, escaped Canady's gun, and was lured and given 500 lashes by Canady's cousins Peter and David Dill; he died, an inquest called it murder, and the grand jury ignored the bill.

framing.detail: The Freeman's Louisville column introduced the case as another of Georgia's 'unpunished murderers' who go free without 'the usual sham trial', called the brothers 'young savages' and 'young brutal savages', and headlined the section 'A Brutal Murder Ignored by the Grand Jury'.

record_check.dossier: A wage dispute ending in a fatal whipping by two sons of the farmer's cousin; no organized band or whitecap disguise is reported, so labor violence by individuals fits better than whitecapping.
Two named brothers, Peter and David Dill, not a mob.
Peter and David Dill, sons of planter Joseph Dill.
Before July 29, 1885, the date of the dispatch; the inquest and grand-jury action had already happened by then, so the whipping may be earlier than July.
The one report is in the New York Freeman, a Black-edited weekly, not the white press.

record_check.record: Two sons of planter Joseph Dill whipped a Black laborer ... inflicting 500 lashes. He died shortly afterward.
record_check.dossier: Supported; add that the sons' father was a cousin of the farmer Canady, that Canady first went for his gun, and that the grand-jury foreman was a Dill/Canady relative.

info: Before July 29, 1885 (date of the dispatch); the whipping, inquest and grand-jury action all preceded it, exact dates not given
An unnamed Black ('colored') man who had worked six months for the farmer Canady without drawing his pay
No crime alleged; the Dill sons 'decided to punish the runaway colored man' after he quit and returned to demand his wages
Peter and David Dill, sons of planter Joseph Dill, a cousin of Canady
1 (died a short time after the whipping)
The Dill sons were reported to be free

sources.note: Louisville correspondence column; paragraph quoting a July 29 special dispatch from Lincoln County to the Louisville Commercial on the whipping death and the ignored grand-jury bill; text has a gap mid-account.
quotes: In the long list of unpunished murderers in Georgia, another one goes free without even an interference of the law or the usual sham trial
Canady cursed, swore and went into the house after his gun. When he returned the man was out of range and made good his escape.
These young savages decided to punish the runaway colored man. They induced him to meet them
by the elder Canada and the elder Dill, that the young brutes desisted, having inflicted 500 lashes.
the foreman of the jury was a relative of the Dills and Canadys and succeeded in getting the bill ignored, and the young brutal savages to-day go free.
